questions.stem: At roughly what top speed do impulses travel along neurones?

options.text: Up to about 100 metres per second
options.explanation: That is the stated top speed of nerve impulses.

options.text: Up to about 10 metres per second
options.explanation: An order of magnitude too slow.

options.text: Up to about 100 metres per hour
options.explanation: Wrong time unit — impulses are far faster.

options.text: Up to about 1000 metres per second
options.explanation: Overshoots the stated figure tenfold.

questions.stem: What form does the message take inside the nervous system?

options.explanation: That is the endocrine route, not the nervous one.
Nervous messages are electrical impulses on nerve cells.
No such transmission exists in this system.
That is transport of gas, not of information.

questions.stem: Which example shows the rapid response the nervous system makes possible?

options.text: Healing a cut over a week
options.explanation: Repair takes days and is not nervous control.
Growth is slow and developmental, not a nervous response.

options.text: Jerking a hand back the instant it touches a flame
options.explanation: The withdrawal reflex is the named rapid-response example.
Digestion is chemical and slow.

questions.stem: Which set of components does the nervous system coordinate?

options.explanation: Glands belong to the hormonal side of the comparison.

options.text: Only the muscles of the legs
options.explanation: The loop is body-wide, not limited to limbs.
Blood cells are carriers, not coordinated responders here.

options.text: Sensory receptors, central decision-making centres and effectors
options.explanation: All three are coordinated in one loop by the nervous system.

questions.stem: Which function is best handled by nervous rather than hormonal control?

options.text: An instant withdrawal from a hot surface
options.explanation: Instant responses are exactly the nervous system's specialty.
Metabolic pacing suits hormonal control.

options.text: Adjusting body chemistry over many hours
options.explanation: Slow adjustments suit hormones.
Growth is developmental, not instant control.

questions.stem: State the message type and the cells that carry it in the nervous system.
questions.modelAnswer: Electrical impulses, carried along nerve cells called neurones.

questions.stem: Give the top speed at which impulses travel.
questions.modelAnswer: Up to about 100 metres per second.

questions.stem: Explain why a withdrawal reflex cannot rely on hormonal communication.
questions.modelAnswer: Hormones move at blood-flow speed and must circulate before acting, whereas an impulse reaches about 100 metres per second along neurones; a hand on a flame would be burned before any hormone could arrive, so only electrical signalling is fast enough for protection.

questions.stem: A student's finger brushes a hot kettle and pulls away at once. Name the route the fastest signal took and the organs that acted as effector.
questions.modelAnswer: The signal ran as electrical impulses along sensory neurones into the central nervous system and out along motor neurones; the effectors were the arm muscles, which contracted to withdraw the finger.

questions.stem: How do hormones travel around the body?

options.explanation: Neurones carry electrical impulses, not hormones.
Hormones are carried by the blood and circulate body-wide.
The named route is the bloodstream.
No such tubes exist; glands release into blood.

questions.stem: What kind of message does the endocrine system send?

options.explanation: Light is a stimulus, not an internal message.
That is the nervous system's medium.
Hormones are the chemical substances of endocrine control.
No acoustic signalling exists between organs.

questions.stem: On what does a hormone act once it circulates?

options.text: On the gland that released it only
options.explanation: The action happens at targets elsewhere in the body.
Hormones act on target organs of many kinds.
Effects are specific to target organs, not universal.
Hormones alter the activity of specific target organs.

questions.stem: Which pairing from the nervous-versus-endocrine comparison is correct?

options.text: Nervous action is very fast; endocrine action is slower
options.explanation: That is the speed-of-action row of the table.

options.text: Nervous effects last long; endocrine effects stop quickly
options.explanation: Reversed duration — hormones last longer.

options.text: Nervous message is chemical; endocrine message is electrical
options.explanation: The types are the wrong way round.

options.text: Nervous effect is widespread; endocrine effect is localised
options.explanation: Reversed — hormones act widely, nerves locally.

questions.stem: Why do hormonal effects outlast nervous ones?

options.explanation: Glands secrete chemicals, not impulses.

options.text: Because hormones continue acting until they are broken down
options.explanation: Duration ends only when the hormone is broken down.

options.text: Because nerves fire for hours at a time
options.explanation: Nervous effects stop quickly.

options.text: Because hormones replicate inside target cells
options.explanation: Hormones do not reproduce.

questions.stem: State what endocrine glands produce and the collective name for them.
questions.modelAnswer: They produce and secrete hormones; together the glands form the endocrine system.

questions.stem: Give the two message-transmission routes named in the comparison table.
questions.modelAnswer: Nervous messages travel along neurones; hormonal messages travel through the bloodstream in plasma.

questions.stem: Explain why one hormone secretion can affect several organs at once.
questions.modelAnswer: Because hormones ride the circulating blood, a single secretion is delivered to every organ the blood reaches; any organ with matching target receptors responds, so one signal can change the activity of several targets simultaneously — unlike a nerve impulse, which is aimed along specific neurones.

questions.stem: During a long walk your heart rate stays elevated for many minutes. Which control system fits this sustained adjustment, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: The hormonal (endocrine) system fits: sustained adjustments suit chemical messengers that circulate and keep acting until broken down, whereas nervous control is reserved for instant, short-lived commands.
